hints: Notice each option uses a different energy formula with the numbers $60 \text{ kg}$ and $40 \text{ m}$, $160 \text{ W}$ and $15 \text{ s}$, $12 \text{ kg}$ and $20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $120 \text{ kPa}$ and $0.020 \text{ m}^3$.
Recall the four governing relations: $mgh$ for gravitational potential change, $Pt$ for power-time energy, $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ for kinetic energy, and $p\Delta V$ for pressure-volume work.
Calculate each value in joules, remembering to convert $120 \text{ kPa}$ to $120000 \text{ Pa}$, and look for the one that gives $24000 \text{ J}$ instead of $2400 \text{ J}$.
walkthrough: List the formula needed for each amount: $\Delta E_p = mgh$, $E = Pt$, $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, and $W = p\Delta V$.

Check the three that equal $2400 \text{ J}$: $Pt = 160 \times 15 = 2400 \text{ J}$, $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 0.5 \times 12 \times (20)^2 = 6 \times 400 = 2400 \text{ J}$, and $p\Delta V = (120 \times 10^3) \times 0.020 = 2400 \text{ J}$.
Calculate the gravitational change using $g \approx 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ or $10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$: $mgh = 60 \times 9.81 \times 40 \approx 23544 \text{ J}$, about $24000 \text{ J}$.
Only the $60 \text{ kg}$ falling through $40 \text{ m}$ does not give $2400 \text{ J}$ because it is a factor of 10 too large. This is option A.

options.A: Decrease in $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h \approx 60 \times 10 \times 40 = 24000 \text{ J}$, which is ten times larger than $2400 \text{ J}$.
options.B: Energy from power is $E = Pt = 160 \times 15 = 2400 \text{ J}$, so it is $2400 \text{ J}$.
options.C: Kinetic energy is $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 0.5 \times 12 \times 20^2 = 2400 \text{ J}$, so it is $2400 \text{ J}$.
options.D: Work by gas is $W = p\Delta V = 120000 \times 0.020 = 2400 \text{ J}$, so it is $2400 \text{ J}$.
